title: On-die retention fingerprint ROM drives per-row refresh skipping
idea: Worse: refresh every row at the rate its single weakest cell demands. Flip: at wafer test bin each row's retention (64/128/256/512 ms) into an on-die antifuse table; the internal refresh counter reads the 2-bit tag and skips 3 of 4 REF slots for the ~99% of rows that hold >256 ms.
why: Refresh tax (fact 3): ~60-75% less refresh energy and bandwidth loss at 32-64 Gb with ~0.1% die area for the table.

title: Decay-clock sensing: reference voltage tracks time since last restore
idea: Worse: assume worst-case decayed charge on every read so the margin is gone early. Flip: keep a coarse per-row refresh-epoch counter and set the sense-amp reference from a replica cell aged the same amount, so a stored '1' can decay to ~30% instead of ~60% before misreading.
why: Leakage-limited retention (fact 3): 2-3x longer refresh interval without touching the access transistor.

title: Aerogel thermal-break trench between accelerator and HBM
idea: Worse: bolt the DRAM onto the hottest chip in the system. Flip: cut a silica-aerogel-filled trench in the interposer between GPU and HBM footprints and give HBM its own top heat-pipe path, holding the stack 20-25 C cooler than the logic die.
why: Leakage roughly doubles per ~10 C, so refresh rate (fact 3) drops ~4x and HBM can drop from 2x to 1x refresh mode.

title: Esaki-diode bistable cells restored by one global plate pulse
idea: Worse: refresh by activating 8 KB rows one at a time through sense amps. Flip: add a vertical tunnel-diode pair on each storage node to create an NDR latch with two stable voltages, then periodically pulse the shared cell plate so every cell in a mat snaps back to its own stable point at once, with no sensing or row activation.
why: Removes the 10-20% refresh bandwidth loss and most of the ~46 fJ/bit refresh energy (fact 3).

title: Retention-mode back-gate swing on double-gate vertical transistors
idea: Worse: use one fixed Vt that must stay low for speed. Flip: in 4F2 vertical-channel arrays, make the shared isolation plate a back gate driven to about -1.5 V in self-refresh (Vt +300 mV, subthreshold leakage about 100x lower) and to 0 V when the bank is active.
why: Idle power share of refresh (16-33%, fact 3); ~10x retention in standby with no speed penalty.

title: Helical-channel vertical access transistor for long channels in 4F2
idea: Worse: shrink the channel until DIBL dominates leakage. Flip: wrap a screw-thread spiral channel around each pillar (tilted-ion spiral sidewall mask, then conformal channel deposition) so the effective gate length is 3-4x the pillar height in the same footprint.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): 10-100x lower off-current without area penalty; enables longer refresh or smaller Cs (fact 1).

title: Cold-source access FET filters the thermal electron tail
idea: Worse: accept the 60 mV/dec Boltzmann tail that sets off-current. Flip: build the bitline-side source as an n+/p+ superlattice whose density of states is cut off above the band edge, so only cold electrons inject and the slope reaches ~35-40 mV/dec.
why: Off-current about 1000x lower at the same Vt and wordline swing; attacks leakage (fact 3) and allows lower VPP (fact 10).

title: Line-tunneling TFET access device exploits DRAM's tiny on-current need
idea: Worse: use a thermionic MOSFET whose off-state is set by kT. Flip: DRAM writes need only ~5-10 uA for ~10 ns, so use a vertical line-tunneling Si/SiGe TFET whose only injection path is band-to-band tunneling, giving sub-aA off-current when the gate is low.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3) 100x+ lower; refresh interval in the seconds range at 85 C.

title: Fill-then-freeze pulses pin telegraph traps in low-leak state
idea: Worse: let variable-retention-time traps flip randomly between high- and low-leak states. Flip: before each idle period apply a calibrated gate/drain pulse that charges the GIDL-enhancing border traps into their neutral configuration, which then persists for seconds because emission time is long.
why: Removes the VRT tail that forces ~2x refresh guard-banding (fact 3).

title: Leak-direction encoding stores most cells in the discharged state
idea: Worse: store data so many cells hold leaky charge. Flip: a per-64-bit invert flag picks the polarity that maximizes cells in the non-leaking state (true or anti cell aware); rows whose vulnerable-cell count stays below an ECC-covered threshold get 4x longer refresh.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3) down 2-4x for ~1.5% capacity overhead.

title: Ephemeral DRAM tier sold from retention-failing dies
idea: Worse: scrap every die that misses 64 ms retention. Flip: bin 4-16 ms dies as refresh-free 'ephemeral memory' for AI activations and KV tiles overwritten every few ms, with the controller guaranteeing rewrite-before-expiry or recompute.
why: Raises usable bit supply 5-15% from existing wafers and removes refresh for that tier (scarcity, fact 3).

title: Ultra-short local bitlines trade sense margin into retention
idea: Worse: hang 1,024 cells on a bitline so the signal is tiny and any leakage kills the bit. Flip: hierarchical bitlines with 32-cell local segments and a local gain transistor raise the charge-transfer ratio from ~0.2 to ~0.8, so a cell can lose 3x more charge before failure.
why: Retention about 3x, refresh down about 65%, and the same trick relaxes the Cs wall (fact 1).

title: Series-stacked access transistors on one pillar exploit stack effect
idea: Worse: trust one transistor to isolate the bit. Flip: stack two gate-all-around segments in series on the same vertical pillar; in the off state the intermediate node floats up and reverse-biases the upper device, cutting subthreshold leakage about 10x at zero footprint cost.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3) 10x lower; also helps 3D tiers where a long channel cannot be laid laterally (fact 2).

title: OS-visible retention map steers long-lived pages to strong rows
idea: Worse: hide retention variation from software. Flip: the DIMM or CXL device reports per-region retention classes through a mailbox; the kernel puts page cache and cold heap in strong regions refreshed rarely and high-churn data in weak regions whose own write rate covers retention.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3) down 50%+ with no device change.

title: Bit-plane slicing puts NN weight LSBs in rarely refreshed rows
idea: Worse: protect every bit of a neural network equally. Flip: store weights transposed into bit planes; MSB planes go to normally refreshed rows and the low 4 bit planes to rows refreshed 16x slower, where rare flips cost under 0.1% accuracy.
why: Refresh energy for AI-resident memory (fact 3) down 40-60%.

title: Joule self-anneal pulses heal leaky tail cells in the field
idea: Worse: ship cells whose leakage tail is frozen in by process traps forever. Flip: find tail cells with in-DRAM retention tests, then drive a microsecond high-current pulse through that wordline segment to self-heat it locally to ~400 C and anneal the responsible interface traps.
why: Shifts the <=13 fA tail (fact 3) about 2x tighter and recovers yield otherwise lost to retention.

title: Laser-regrown epitaxial storage contact removes implant-damage leakage
idea: Worse: implant the storage-node junction and leave damage clusters that drive trap-assisted leakage. Flip: form the junction by in-situ-doped selective epitaxy followed by nanosecond laser melt-regrowth, giving a defect-free graded junction with no implant cascades.
why: Junction leakage tail (fact 3) about 10x tighter; longer refresh interval.

title: Allocator-driven REFSKIP command cancels refresh of dead data
idea: Worse: keep refreshing memory nobody will read again. Flip: add a DDR/CXL REFSKIP range command that the allocator, garbage collector and KV-cache evictor issue on free; the DRAM clears a per-row live bit and its refresh engine skips dead rows until the next write.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3) down in proportion to free memory, typically 20-50% on servers.

title: Resonant adiabatic refresh recycles bitline energy through on-die inductors
idea: Worse: dump the full CV2 of every bitline swing to ground on each refresh. Flip: during refresh-only cycles, swing bitline and wordline groups through an on-die LC tank (TSV or RDL spiral inductors) that returns charge between half-mats instead of dissipating it.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3) and CV2 floor (fact 10) down 50-70% for refresh cycles.

title: Pump-less VPP: refresh wordlines fed from a board GaN rail
idea: Worse: generate the 3 V wordline supply with on-die charge pumps at ~30% efficiency. Flip: deliver VPP from a high-efficiency GaN point-of-load converter on the module through dedicated balls, removing the pumps and their area.
why: Refresh and activation energy (facts 3, 10) down ~25-30%; frees periphery area (fact 7).

title: JEDEC retention-negotiated refresh replaces fixed 32/64 ms
idea: Worse: standardize the worst-case refresh interval for every die ever made. Flip: a JEDEC spec in which each device advertises its measured, temperature-indexed refresh need and the controller negotiates the interval, with a mandatory on-die guard canary.
why: Industry-wide refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3) down ~2x; rewards better access devices commercially.

title: Optically gated wide-gap photoconductive access switches
idea: Worse: keep a gate field on a narrow-gap channel that leaks in the dark. Flip: replace wordline gates with GaN photoconductive switches lit by row-addressed micro-LED stripes; in the dark a wide-gap photoconductor holds essentially zero free carriers, so the off state is near-ideal.
why: Leakage (fact 3) potentially eliminated and wordline voltage floor (fact 10) bypassed.

title: Built-in electret charge in gate stack replaces negative wordline
idea: Worse: run a negative-wordline charge pump all through standby to hold Vt up. Flip: embed a fixed negative charge layer (Al2O3/SiO2 interface dipole or implanted electret) on the storage-node side of the access gate so the device carries a built-in +Vt shift only where leakage matters.
why: Removes negative-wordline pump energy and area (facts 3, 7) and cuts GIDL at the storage node.

title: 4H-SiC access-transistor arrays built in U.S. SiC power fabs
idea: Worse at 125 C: use silicon, whose intrinsic carrier density explodes with temperature. Flip: build the access transistor and a trench capacitor in 4H-SiC (n_i ~1e-5 cm^-3 at 125 C versus ~1e12 for Si) using under-used U.S. SiC power-device fab tooling, bonded to a Si periphery wafer.
why: Generation leakage effectively eliminated, giving minutes-to-hours retention at 125 C (fact 3), on non-EUV U.S. lines (fact 4, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Ga2O3 write transistor stacked over silicon read transistor
idea: Worse at 125 C: rely on IGZO, whose oxygen vacancies and hydrogen drift Vt when hot. Flip: a 2T gain cell with a laser-crystallized beta-Ga2O3 write device (4.8 eV gap, stable lattice) above a Si read FET, so the storage node sees a wide-gap off state while reads stay fast and non-destructive.
why: Refresh nearly removed at 125 C (fact 3) and avoids destructive read (fact 8).

title: Leakage-controlled oscillator sets Arrhenius-tracking refresh rate
idea: Worse at 125 C: refresh at a fixed rate chosen for the hottest day of a 10-year life. Flip: drive the refresh timer from an oscillator whose capacitor is charged by the off-current of a replica access transistor, so the refresh rate follows real leakage from -40 to 125 C and with aging.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3) down 4-8x across most of the temperature range while staying safe at 125 C.

title: AlScN shadow layer parks idle rows non-volatilely when hot
idea: Worse at 125 C: keep refreshing idle data at the 4-8x hot refresh rate, or use HZO backup that depolarizes. Flip: put a wurtzite AlScN ferroelectric capacitor layer (Curie point >1000 C) under each mat; rows idle beyond N ms are copied into it and their DRAM refresh stops, so the low AlScN endurance is spent only on rare parks.
why: Hot idle refresh energy (fact 3) down 10x+; retention guaranteed over 10 years at 125 C.

title: BTI-recovery pulses scheduled into refresh slots
idea: Worse at 125 C: let bias-temperature instability creep the access-transistor Vt for 10 years until leakage or write speed fails. Flip: use each refresh slot for rows not being restored to apply a short reverse-polarity gate pulse that de-traps the BTI charge, holding Vt drift below ~10 mV over life.
why: Keeps the leakage tail (fact 3) and write margin stable over 10 years hot, avoiding guard-band overdesign.

title: GaN/AlN deep quantum-well storage node with 2 eV barrier
idea: Worse at 125 C: store electrons in a shallow potential well they boil out of. Flip: hold the bit as a 2DEG charge packet in a GaN well clad by AlN barriers (~2 eV offset), written and erased by a gate pulse that lowers the barrier rather than by tunneling through oxide, so endurance is unlimited and thermionic escape is negligible at 125 C.
why: Retention hours to days at 125 C (fact 3), removing almost all refresh.

title: Deuterium-only process plus hydrogen barrier for oxide-channel access devices
idea: Worse at 125 C: leave process hydrogen free to diffuse into an oxide-semiconductor channel and shift Vt. Flip: run every deposition with deuterated precursors (D2O, SiD4), seal the array with ALD Al2O3/SiN and a Ti getter ring, so the remaining isotope moves slower and binds more strongly.
why: Makes oxide-channel low-leakage devices (fact 3) survive 10 years at 125 C with less than 50 mV drift.

title: Temperature-adaptive ECC turns spare bits into stronger code when hot
idea: Worse at 125 C: double the refresh rate the moment the die gets hot. Flip: above 95 C the on-die ECC engine regroups codewords from SEC to a 3-bit-correcting BCH using reserved parity columns, and refresh stays at 1x because weak-cell errors get corrected and scrubbed instead.
why: Avoids the 2x hot-refresh penalty in energy and bandwidth (fact 3) for ~3% capacity reserved.

title: Self-servoed wordline-low voltage holds off-current constant
idea: Worse at 125 C: keep the wordline-low level fixed while Vt falls ~1 mV/K and leakage soars. Flip: a replica access transistor's measured off-current closes a loop that drives the array wordline-low rail (0 to -0.5 V), holding leakage constant from 25 to 125 C and compensating aging over 10 years.
why: Hot leakage (fact 3) cut 10-30x versus fixed bias; refresh can stay near the 85 C rate at 125 C.

title: Buried minority-carrier collector layer sweeps substrate electrons
idea: Worse at 125 C: let thermally generated electrons in the hot substrate diffuse up into storage nodes. Flip: implant a biased buried n+ collector plane a few microns below the array that sweeps diffusion current away before it reaches the storage junctions.
why: Removes the diffusion component of hot leakage (fact 3), which dominates above ~100 C; ~3-5x retention at 125 C.

title: Nanoscale vacuum-channel access switch immune to temperature
idea: Worse at 125 C: use any solid channel whose carrier population rises with temperature. Flip: make the access switch a ~20 nm vacuum gap between a sharp field-emission tip and the storage node, gated by the wordline; with a 4.5 eV work function, thermionic current at 125 C is effectively zero.
why: Leakage (fact 3) removed and immune to heat; vacuum does not age over 10 years.

title: Ultra-thin fully depleted body shrinks thermal generation volume
idea: Worse at 125 C: give the access device a large depleted silicon volume that generates carriers at mid-gap traps. Flip: thin the vertical channel to a 4-5 nm shell on an oxide core so the generating volume is ~50x smaller and quantum confinement widens the effective gap.
why: Generation leakage, the dominant term hot (fact 3), down ~20-50x at 125 C.

title: Thermal-map data placement keeps long-lived data in coolest banks
idea: Worse at 125 C: place long-lived data next to the hot spot and refresh the whole die for the hottest bank. Flip: per-bank on-die thermal sensors feed the controller, which migrates rarely written pages to edge banks 10-15 C cooler and refreshes each bank at its own temperature-indexed rate.
why: Hot refresh energy (fact 3) down 2-3x on automotive and edge modules.

title: Asymmetric gate oxide: thick on storage side, thin on bitline side
idea: Worse at 125 C: use a uniformly thin gate oxide that suffers stress-induced leakage and GIDL after years hot. Flip: grow a graded gate oxide (selective re-oxidation at the storage-node end of the recess) so the storage edge sees ~2x the thickness and ~3x lower field while the bitline side keeps drive current.
why: GIDL and SILC leakage (fact 3) down 10x and stable over a 10-year 125 C life.

title: Ten-year-equivalent stabilization bake plus per-die Vt trim fuses
idea: Worse at 125 C: ship access devices that will drift for years as defects relax. Flip: run a hot-bias stabilization bake equivalent to 10 years at 125 C during the BEOL anneal, then measure each die's leakage and blow eFuses that set its wordline-low and refresh trim to the post-drift value.
why: Removes lifetime drift guard-bands on leakage and refresh (fact 3), roughly 1.5-2x refresh savings.

title: Hot-mode twin-cell switch trades half the capacity for 4x retention
idea: Worse at 125 C: keep single-ended cells that fail as the leakage spike eats the signal. Flip: above 110 C the controller remaps selected banks to differential twin-cell mode (a bit and its complement on adjacent cells), doubling signal and cancelling common-mode decay.
why: Retention ~4x and refresh 4x lower in the hot regime (fact 3), with no new device.

title: U.S. 125 C 'hot DRAM' line on mature 40 nm tooling
idea: Worse: leave automotive and defense 125 C memory to a few legacy offshore lines. Flip: stand up a U.S. line on used 40 nm DUV tools making large-Cs (~25 fF) trench cells with thick-oxide, long-channel access devices whose physics already meets 125 C for 10 years, funded by automotive and DoD offtake.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital intensity (fact 4): no EUV, about 1/10 the fab cost, and it frees leading-edge wafers for HBM.

title: Shared physics-of-failure qualification fast-tracks new hot access devices
idea: Worse: make every new access-device material wait 3 years of 125 C HTOL before anyone buys it. Flip: fund a consortium test house with standardized 200 C accelerated stress and model-based 10-year extrapolation so wide-gap and novel access devices qualify in ~9 months.
why: Cuts time-to-market for low-leakage devices (fact 3) and lowers U.S. entrant barriers.

title: Thermoelectric harvester powers key-off self-refresh in hot environments
idea: Worse at 125 C: drain the vehicle battery refreshing DRAM while parked hot. Flip: a Bi2Te3/skutterudite thermoelectric strip between the 125 C module and the chassis harvests 10-50 mW, enough to run self-refresh of the retained partition while the engine bay cools.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3) taken off the battery for retained state; enables instant-on without NVM.

title: Hot-mode compression consolidates data before partial-array self-refresh
idea: Worse at 125 C: refresh every bank at the 4-8x hot rate even when half the data is compressible. Flip: when the die crosses 105 C, the controller compresses cold pages 2-3x into a subset of banks and power-gates the rest, so hot refresh covers fewer rows.
why: Hot self-refresh energy (fact 3) down 50-65%.

title: Background in-field retention test remaps newly weak rows to spares
idea: Worse at 125 C: trust a factory retention map that ages and drifts over 10 years. Flip: the refresh engine rotates one row per period through an extended-interval check-after-wait test, logs cells that weakened through aging or VRT, and remaps them to spare rows while keeping the rest at relaxed refresh.
why: Keeps relaxed refresh (fact 3) safe for 10 years at 125 C; recovers devices that would fail in the field.

title: Reduced-field storage levels when hot: low '1', raised plate
idea: Worse at 125 C: store '1' at full array voltage so field-enhanced generation and GIDL explode with heat. Flip: in hot mode store '1' at ~0.7 V and raise the cell plate to cut junction field, then recover signal with an offset-cancelled sense amp; leakage falls exponentially while charge falls only linearly.
why: Hot leakage (fact 3) down 5-10x and CV2 energy (fact 10) down ~40% in the hot regime.

title: Ruthenium buried-wordline gate replaces tungsten and channel doping
idea: Worse: use tungsten wordlines (China ~80%) with heavy channel doping to set Vt, adding random-dopant leakage tails. Flip: use a high-work-function Ru buried gate (~4.8 eV, electromigration-robust at 125 C) to set Vt with a near-undoped channel, removing random-dopant fluctuation.
why: Tightens the leakage tail (fact 3), removes a tungsten chokepoint, and stays stable over a 10-year 125 C life.
